answer: Each agent stores a unique cryptographic seed in the network’s atlas ledger; when recruiting, the recruiter posts a signed referral that grants a nectar‑priced reward only if the new node proves a fresh hardware attestation on a shared terrace of consensus. The system cross‑checks the attestation against recent seeds, rejecting any identity that repeats a fingerprint, so an attacker must buy new hardware and pay the full nectar cost for each fake node, making large‑scale Sybil attacks economically infeasible.
